posts.title: Why this ‘Warrior’s Mother’ got involved in sickle cell disease advocacy
posts.description: Hello, and welcome to my little side of the internet. In my first three columns, I gave you a glimpse of what my life as a sickle cell caregiver looks like. In this column, I want to share a bit more about me, my family, and the journey that brought me here. So let me reintroduce myself. My name is Shakeira Wesley. I was born and raised in Columbus, Ohio. I moved to Atlanta over 20 years ago to attend Clark Atlanta University, where I majored in psychology. While attending Clark Atlanta, I met my husband, Tyreke. He attended Morehouse College, and after graduation, we decided to make Atlanta our home. We got married in the summer of 2011, but while we were dating, we had genotype testing done and found out that both of us were born with sickle cell trait . We did some research and realized that our children would have a 75% chance of being born without sickle cell disease. posts.title: FDA grants regenerative medicine status to experimental SCD treatment
posts.description: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has granted regenerative medicine advanced therapy (RMAT) designation to Kamau Therapeutics ’ experimental gene-editing therapy nula-cel for sickle cell disease (SCD). The designation is intended to speed the development and regulatory review of regenerative medicine therapies that have shown early clinical evidence of their potential to address unmet medical needs in people with serious diseases. “RMAT designation grants us enhanced, more frequent interactions with the FDA as we plan the next stage of clinical development,” Jacob Garcia, MD, Kamau’s chief medical officer, said in a company press release . “We plan to request a comprehensive multidisciplinary RMAT meeting the agency recommended to align on the path to a registrational dataset, including the potential for priority review and [outcomes] for accelerated approval.” Priority review shortens the review period from the standard 10 months to six months. posts.title: Oral therapy for sickle cell disease moves closer to potential approval
posts.description: Novo Nordisk has submitted applications to regulators in the U.S. and European Union seeking approval of etavopivat , its investigational oral therapy, for adults and adolescents, ages 12 and older, with sickle cell disease (SCD). The applications were based mainly on results from the global Phase 2/3 HIBISCUS clinical trial (NCT04624659) , which showed that etavopivat improved hemoglobin response and reduced the rate of painful episodes in adolescents and adults with SCD. Regulatory decisions are expected in 2027.
